background.definition: Vitreous hemorrhage (VH) is the presence of extravasated blood in the vitreous cavity of the eye, defined as the space between the posterior lens capsule and the surface of the retina.

list.listitem: Dense spontaneous first-time vitreous hemorrhage: 7 cases/100,000/year.
Approximately 60% to 90% of all cases are caused by proliferative diabetic retinopathy, posterior vitreous detachment (PVD) with or without retinal tear or detachment, and ocular trauma.
Trauma, including shaken baby syndrome, is the leading cause in younger patients, and proliferative sickle cell retinopathy is the leading nondiabetic cause in black patients.

Other causes include retinal vein occlusion, retinal macroaneurysm, macular degeneration, hypertensive retinopathy, complication of intraocular surgery, Terson syndrome, intraocular tumor, Eales disease, Coats' disease, retinopathy of prematurity, retinal angiomatosis, retinal cavernous hemangioma, bleeding diathesis, and others.
A growing cause is blunt trauma from the deployment of airbags, with vitreous and retinal hemorrhage accounting for 25% of ocular injuries from airbags.
In a case series of spontaneous vitreous hemorrhage among 76 children, vasculitis and hematologic disorders were the most common etiology.

Sources of hemorrhage into the vitreous include: (1) bleeding from diseased or abnormal blood vessels; (2) mechanical disruption of normal retinal vessels; and (3) extension of hemorrhage through the retina from other sources, including subretinal bleeding from macular degeneration or choroidal melanoma.
Retinal tears are important to diagnose early as prompt intervention may prevent the development of retinal detachments and permanent loss of vision. B
A complete ocular examination of both eyes should be conducted. C
B-scan ultrasound should be performed when the view of the fundus is obscured, and can be pivotal in establishing the diagnosis and influencing the management plan. B
The possibility of shaken baby syndrome or traumatic child abuse must be considered in infants and children. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Inflammatory cells in vitreous. No red blood cells in vitreous.
Can occur without VH, but present with similar symptoms. No red blood cells in vitreous.

list.listitem: Patients usually present with sudden painless loss or decrease of vision, or the appearance of floaters, cobwebs, or haze.

A complete ocular examination of both eyes should be conducted, including visual acuity testing, intraocular pressures, and assessment of pupils. A mild relative afferent pupillary defect may be observed. Slit lamp examination should be done prior to dilation to assess for iris neovascularization.
Critical signs after dilation include red blood cells in the vitreous. These can be identified at the slit lamp by focusing behind the posterior lens capsule with the slit beam at an oblique angle.

Direct ophthalmoscopy will often reveal red floating debris and a loss of fundus detail such as optic nerve and retinal vessels. The red reflex of the fundus may be obscured with a severe hemorrhage and there may be no view of the fundus. Chronic VH may have a yellow ochre appearance due to hemoglobin breakdown.
Examination of the fellow eye may reveal clues to the etiology of the VH, including diabetic or hypertensive retinopathy, macular degeneration, or vasculitis.
Indirect ophthalmoscopy including scleral depression to assess for peripheral retinal tears should be conducted by a trained ophthalmologist.

B-scan ultrasound should be performed when the view of the fundus is obscured. A dynamic and static ultrasound may reveal gross pathology such as an intraocular tumor, a retinal detachment, or a large choroidal neovascular membrane. Occasionally, the B-scan may identify neovascular fronds or a flap tear when conducted with concomitant scleral depression. However, their absence on B-scan does not rule out their presence.
Intravenous fluorescein angiography may aid in determining the etiology of the hemorrhage, but the quality of the images will depend on the density of the hemorrhage.
CT or MRI may be indicated in patient's with suspected Terson syndrome to evaluate for intracranial hemorrhage.
Long-bone skeletal survey may be indicated in suspected child abuse cases.
Laboratory testing may include a blood glucose test, as VH can be the presenting sign of diabetes mellitus. Coagulation studies may be indicated by history.
See for a suggested approach to the evaluation of suspected vitreous hemorrhage.
An emergent ophthalmic consultation should be obtained if a retinal tear or break is suspected or if there is a history of ocular trauma or suspected abuse. C
Treatment of vitreous hemorrhage involves treatment of the underlying cause of the VH, the VH itself, and the possible complications. B

Treatments directed at the underlying etiology include: argon laser retinopexy or cryotherapy to seal retinal breaks, surgical repair of retinal detachments, and argon laser pan-retinal photocoagulation for proliferative retinopathies. The established treatment for nonclearing VH is surgical pars plana vitrectomy. B
Pretreatment with intravitreal bevacizumab and adjunctive panretinal photocoagulation may be used with pars plana vitrectomy. B

The timing of pars plana vitrectomy is determined by the etiology of the VH, the need to clear the hemorrhage to treat the underlying disease process, the status of the fellow eye, and the functional needs of the patient. B

Proliferative diabetic retinopathy is mediated in part by vascular endothelial growth factor. New modalities in the pharmacological treatment of VH include bevacizumab (Avastin) and ranibizumab (Lucentis), anti-VEGF drugs that can be administered directly into the vitreous. They have been used to increase the absorption of VH to delay or even avoid surgery and as an adjunct to surgical intervention to decrease the risk of postoperative VH.

A systematic review identified 5 RCTs comparing anti-VEGF monotherapy with panretinal photocoagulation and found potential benefits of anti-VEGF for letters gained and lower rates of vitrectomy and hemorrhage.

A more recent high quality study randomized 205 participants with vitreous hemorrhage due to proliferative diabetic retinopathy to intravitreous aflibercept or to vitrectomy with panretinal photocoagulation. At 24 weeks, there were trends favoring vitrectomy with PRP with a mean visual acuity letter score 59.3 with aflibercept and 63 with vitrectomy, difference -5, 95% CI -10.2 to 0.3, p = 0.06. However, there was no difference at 2 years and no difference in the need for subsequent treatments.

Intraveiteal bevacizumab prior to vitrectomy in proliferative diabetic retinopathy is associated with a decrease in surgical time, intraoperative bleeding, and vitreous hemorrhage compared to vitrectomy without bevacizumab. However,intraveiteal bevacizumab after surgery for proliferative diabetic retinopathy is not associated with improved rates of hemorrhage or an improvement in visual acuity.

Other medical treatments have aimed to hasten the clearance of VH by accelerating fibrinolysis, hemolysis, vitreous liquefaction, or phagocytosis. The main limitation of these enzymatic accelerators has been toxicity to the retina.
Surgical pars plana vitrectomy has been shown to be effective in treating nonclearing VH.

Early pars plana vitrectomy for diabetic VH is indicated if there is iris neovascularization or suspected proliferative diabetic retinopathy and no history of photocoagulation. Early pars plana vitrectomy should be considered in patients with history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye as the incidence of retinal detachment in the second eye presenting with VH from PVD is 75%. Early pars plana vitrectomy for traumatic VH is considered if there is a risk of endophthalmitis or there is an iron- or copper-containing intraocular foreign body with a potential for retinal toxicity. In infants, early pars plana vitrectomy may be needed to prevent amblyopia from myopic shift from monocular deprivation from a dense VH.
Prior to surgical intervention, the potential visual acuity behind a dense VH may be assessed by 10-Hertz flash visual evoked potential or bright-flash electroretinography.
Major complications of vitrectomy include iatrogenic retinal breaks, progressive cataract, and recurrent vitreous hemorrhage.

A trial randomized 258 patients undergoing pars plana vitrectomy to internal limiting membrane peeling or no peeling. The intervention group had better vision, required fewer post-operative diabetic macular edema treatments, and was less likely to develop an epiretinal membrane 6 months later.

A Chinese observational study in 103 patients undergoing pars plana vitrectomy for diabetic vitreous hemorrhage found a reduced rate of rebleeding and better visual acuity with the addition of intravitreal injection of ranibizumab. However, this has not been studied in a randomized trial with selection bias being a major limitation (the decision for injection was left to patient and physician).
A systematic review of patients with abusive trauma and retinal complications requiring surgery found good outcomes overall, but improved visul acuity when performed within 4 weeks of injury.
Bed rest with head of bed elevated, with or without bilateral patching, allows the blood to settle in the inferior vitreous and may decrease the risk of rebleed.

This decreases the amount of blood that will become suspended in the vitreous, which takes longer to clear, and also increases the visibility of the posterior pole and especially of the superior retina, a common location for retinal breaks that lead to dense VH.
The most common complication of VH is the continued decrease of vision from slow clearing of the hemorrhage.
In infants younger than 2.5 years this may result in amblyopia.
Nonclearing or severe VH can also lead to hemosiderosis bulbi, proliferative vitreoretinopathy, and glaucoma.
Glaucoma is first managed by medical lowering of intraocular pressure and then anterior chamber washout. If these measurements fail, then pars plana vitrectomy may be needed.
Most VH clear spontaneously. B
The natural history and prognosis depend on the underlying etiology of the VH. Diabetic retinopathy and macular degeneration have the worst prognosis. B
Most VH clear spontaneously.
Untreated VH from diabetic retinopathy has a very poor prognosis with 49% of patients having worse than hand-motions vision 3 to 10 years later.
Natural history of VH from retinal arterial macroaneurysm is very good with respect to improved vision, and rebleeds from the same macroaneurysm are very rare.
Nonclearing or severe VH can lead to hemosiderosis bulbi, proliferative vitreoretinopathy, and glaucoma.

Generally, etiologies with no tendency for recurrent bleeding, such as PVD, have a good prognosis for clearing of VH and improvement of vision. Diabetic retinopathy and macular degeneration have the worst prognosis.

Patients with proliferative sickle cell retinopathy have a higher risk of rebleed than patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy. However, VH from sickle cell retinopathy rarely results in permanent vision loss, mainly because the location of hemorrhage is usually more peripheral.
The prognosis for visual acuity in the setting of shaken baby syndrome may be limited by concomitant neurological injury.
If the etiology of the VH cannot be determined, monitor the patient closely as an outpatient.
Warn patients of symptoms of retinal detachment, including flashes of light, new floaters, and a sensation of a cloud or curtain blocking part or all of the vision.
Follow up with serial dilated fundus examinations and B-scan ultrasounds.

cell.label: Suspected VH: Sudden painless decrease of vision or appearance of floaters, cobwebs, or haze.
Ocular history: trauma, surgeries, underlying retinal diseases including diabetic retinopathy, vascular occlusive disease, history of retinal detachment in fellow eye.
Systemic history: diabetes, hypertension (risk of retinal vein occlusion and retinal macroaneurysm), sickle cell disease, malignancy or bleeding diathesis. Measure blood pressure.
Ocular examination: Red blood cells in vitreous?
Raises suspicion for posterior vitreous detachment or retinal tear.
